fields.title: Load Profile
fields.keyTakeaway: System cost is determined by the peak, not the volume, and the load profile is often cheaper to change with a product decision than to pay for with capacity.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Two systems process 6 million requests per day each. Why does one cost twice as much?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Infrastructure cost is determined by the peak, and revenue by the volume. A product with a sharp peak pays for capacity that idles 20 hours a day. Product decisions can change the load shape, and this is direct savings — but only if the PM knows such a lever exists.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: [[load-profile|Load profile]] is the shape of distribution over time. Three typical ones.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Flat.** B2B services with a global audience. Peak coefficient 1.5–2. Cheap. **Daily.** Consumer products. Peak in the evening or at lunch, almost nothing at night. Coefficient 3–6. **Event-driven.** Peaks tied to events: newsletter, sale, match start. Coefficient 10–50, and this is the most expensive profile.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: Cost is determined by the peak because capacity is reserved for it. Autoscaling smooths the difference, but not completely: a server does not spin up instantly, and the database scales poorly.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: Three product levers that change the shape:
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *Smear the event.* Newsletter not to everyone at once, but in waves of 15 minutes. The peak drops multiple times, the effect for the recipient does not change. *Shift in time.* Partner reports are generated at night, not on demand in the morning. *Postpone optional things.* During a peak, background tasks are queued and processed later.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: Separately — **[[thundering-herd|thundering herd effect]]**: many clients simultaneously request data after an event. The classic is all apps re-requesting data exactly at midnight, or all retrying a request exactly 30 seconds after a failure. Cured by random jitter: interval not 30 seconds, but from 25 to 35.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Daily profile with a coefficient of 5. Plus two event-driven overlays: Monday morning — partner reports, Friday evening — maximum orders.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: The Monday peak was solved by staggering the newsletter: "report is ready" emails go out in waves from 8:00 to 11:00, 100 partners every 20 minutes. The dashboard peak dropped from 400 concurrent reports to 90. Not a single partner noticed the difference — they do not know what minute the email is supposed to arrive.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: This decision took two days and saved more than a month of query optimization.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: The thundering herd effect was caught in the app: feed updates happened on a timer synchronized with the start of the minute. Thousands of apps requested the feed in the exact same second. Jitter of ±20 seconds removed the spike entirely.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Not every peak can be smeared: a sale with limited quantity is synchronous by nature, and trying to stretch it breaks the product idea.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: System cost is determined by the peak, not the volume, and the load profile is often cheaper to change with a product decision than to pay for with capacity.
